title: HTTP Digest Access Authentication
summary: Defines HTTP Digest Access Authentication, a challenge-response scheme in which the client proves it knows a password without sending it in the clear. It updates earlier Digest specifications and supports stronger hash algorithms.

plainLanguage.summary: Basic authentication sends the password across the network in readable form. Digest authentication instead sends a scrambled value that only someone who knows the password can produce. RFC 7616 updates that scheme with stronger hash functions and a way to hide the username.

questions: what does the cnonce parameter do
subtitle: A challenge-response login for HTTP that proves you know a password without sending it, now with SHA-256.

tldr.problem: HTTP needs a way for a client to prove it knows a password without sending the password in the clear, as Basic authentication does.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a one-time nonce in a 401 challenge. The client replies with a digest computed from the username, realm, password, nonce, request method and URI, plus its own client nonce.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7616 adds SHA-256 and SHA-512/256, username hashing and internationalization rules. The RFC calls Digest weak by modern cryptographic standards but far better than Basic.

today: RFC 7616 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015 that obsoletes RFC 2617, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It works alongside RFC 7617, which defines Basic authentication, and RFC 7235, which defines the HTTP authentication framework.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP provides a simple challenge-response authentication mechanism that a server can use to challenge a client request and a client can use to provide authentication information. This document defines the HTTP Digest Authentication scheme that can be used with that mechanism.

The document extends but is generally backward compatible with RFC 2617, and its appendix lists the new capabilities introduced. The details of the challenge-response mechanism itself are specified in the HTTP/1.1 authentication document, RFC 7235. The combination of this document with the definition of the Basic authentication scheme in RFC 7617, the Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info header fields in RFC 7615, and RFC 7235 obsoletes RFC 2617.
sections.plainLanguage: Digest is the older sibling of Basic. It is still there for compatibility, but this version gives it newer hash functions and a few fixes.

sections.title: Overall Operation
sections.content:
The Digest scheme is based on a simple challenge-response paradigm. The server challenges using a nonce value and might indicate that username hashing is supported. A valid response contains an unkeyed digest of the username, the password, the given nonce value, the HTTP method and the requested URI. In this way the password is never sent in the clear, and the username can be hashed, depending on the indication received from the server. The username and password must be prearranged in some fashion that this document does not address.

In practice the exchange looks like this. The client asks for a protected resource. The server replies with a 401 Unauthorized status and a WWW-Authenticate header field carrying the scheme, a realm, a fresh nonce and the algorithm it wants. The client computes the digest and retries the request with an Authorization header field. The server performs the same digest operation and compares the result with the value the client sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a random-looking token, the client turns that token and the password into a single scrambled value, and the server checks the value by doing the same calculation with the password it already knows.

sections.title: The WWW-Authenticate Header Field
sections.content:
If a server receives a request for an access-protected object and an acceptable Authorization header field is not sent, the server responds with a 401 Unauthorized status code and a WWW-Authenticate header field using the Digest scheme. The header field can carry the following parameters.

The realm is a string displayed to users so they know which username and password to use, and it should contain at least the name of the host performing the authentication. The domain parameter is a quoted, space-separated list of URIs defining the protection space. The nonce is a server-specified string which should be uniquely generated each time a 401 response is made, and it is advised that it be Base64 or hexadecimal data. The contents of the nonce are implementation dependent and the quality of the implementation depends on a good choice. A nonce might for example be the Base64 encoding of a timestamp, the HTTP ETag of the requested entity and secret data known only to the server, which lets the server limit the nonce's validity and prevents a replay request for an updated version of the resource.

The opaque is a string of data, specified by the server, that the client should return unchanged in later requests. The stale flag indicates that the previous request was rejected because the nonce was stale, in which case the client may retry with a new response without re-prompting for the username and password. The algorithm parameter names the algorithm used to produce the digest and defaults to MD5 if it is not present. The qop parameter must be used by all implementations and lists the quality of protection values supported, where auth indicates authentication and auth-int indicates authentication with integrity protection. The charset parameter is optional and the only allowed value is UTF-8. The userhash parameter is optional and indicates that the server supports username hashing, with a default value of false.
sections.plainLanguage: The challenge tells the client three things that matter: which password to use, a fresh one-time token, and which hash to calculate with. The token is opaque, so the client just passes it back.

sections.title: The Authorization Header Field
sections.content:
The client is expected to retry the request, passing an Authorization header field line with the Digest scheme. The values of the opaque and algorithm fields must be those supplied in the WWW-Authenticate response header field for the entity being requested.

The request can include the following parameters. The response is a string of hex digits computed as described below; it proves that the user knows a password. The username is the user's name in the specified realm, in plaintext or as a hash in hexadecimal notation, and if the username contains characters not allowed inside the ABNF quoted-string production the username* parameter can be used, though sending both username and username* in the same header option must be treated as an error. The realm and the uri, which is the effective request URI, are repeated from the challenge. The qop parameter indicates what quality of protection the client has applied, and its value must be one of the alternatives the server indicated it supports.

The cnonce parameter must be used by all implementations. It is an opaque quoted ASCII-only string provided by the client and used by both client and server to avoid chosen plaintext attacks, to provide mutual authentication and to give some message integrity protection. The nc parameter must also be used by all implementations. It stands for nonce count and is the hexadecimal count of the number of requests, including the current one, that the client has sent with the nonce value in this request, so the first request after a challenge carries nc=00000001. Its purpose is to let the server detect request replays by keeping its own copy of the count, because if the same nc value is seen twice the request is a replay. The userhash parameter is optional and indicates that the username has been hashed.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply carries the answer, the name, the token the server sent, and two extra values chosen by the client: a random client nonce and a count of how many times the client has used the server's nonce.

sections.title: How the Digest Is Computed
sections.content:
The RFC writes H(data) for the unkeyed digest of the data and KD(secret, data) for the keyed digest, which is H of the secret, a colon and the data. The notation unq(X) means the value of the quoted string X without the surrounding quotes and with quoting slashes removed.

When the qop value is auth or auth-int the response is computed as response = KD( H(A1), unq(nonce) ":" nc ":" unq(cnonce) ":" unq(qop) ":" H(A2) ). For the plain algorithm, A1 is unq(username) ":" unq(realm) ":" passwd. For the session variant, written with a -sess suffix, A1 is computed using the nonce from the challenge and the client nonce from the request: H( unq(username) ":" unq(realm) ":" passwd ) ":" unq(nonce-prime) ":" unq(cnonce-prime). That creates a session key that is different for each authentication session, limiting the amount of material hashed with any one key, and it lets a third-party authentication service be used because the server only needs the hash of the credentials.

If qop is auth or is unspecified, A2 is Method ":" request-uri. If qop is auth-int, A2 is Method ":" request-uri ":" H(entity-body), where the entity body hash is computed before any transfer encoding is applied by the sender and after it has been removed by the recipient, including multipart boundaries and embedded header fields. No white space is allowed in the strings to which the digest function is applied unless that white space exists in the quoted strings or the entity body being digested.

To protect the transport of the username, the server should set the userhash parameter to true. A client that supports it must calculate a hash of the username after any other hash calculation and include the userhash parameter with the value true. The operation is username = H( unq(username) ":" unq(realm) ), using the same algorithm used to hash the credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a hash of three things: a secret value built from the name and password, and a second value built from the request itself. Because the request is mixed in, a captured answer cannot be reused for a different page.

sections.title: Security Protocol Negotiation
sections.content:
It is useful for a server to know which security schemes a client is capable of handling. A server might want to require Digest as its authentication method even if it does not know that the client supports it, and a client is encouraged to fail gracefully if the server specifies only schemes it cannot handle.

When a server receives a request to access a resource it might challenge the client by responding with 401 Unauthorized and one or more WWW-Authenticate header fields. If the server responds with multiple challenges, each one of those challenges must use a different digest algorithm, and the server must add the challenges to the response in order of preference, starting with the most preferred algorithm.

The specification defines SHA2-256, which is mandatory to implement, SHA2-512/256 as a backup algorithm, and MD5 for backward compatibility. When the client receives the first challenge it should use the first challenge it supports, unless a local policy dictates otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can offer several hashes at once, best first, and the client picks the best one it understands. That way an old client still works while a new one gets the stronger hash.

sections.title: Internationalization Considerations
sections.content:
In challenges, servers should use the charset authentication parameter to express the character encoding they expect the user agent to use when generating A1 and when hashing the username. The only allowed value is UTF-8, matched case-insensitively. It indicates that the server expects the username and password to be converted to Unicode Normalization Form C and encoded into octets using the UTF-8 character encoding scheme.

For the username, recipients must support all characters defined in the UsernameCasePreserved profile in RFC 7613, with the exception of the colon character. For the password, recipients must support all characters defined in the OpaqueString profile in RFC 7613. If the user agent does not support the encoding indicated by the server, it can fail the request. When usernames cannot be sent hashed and include non-ASCII characters, clients can include the username* parameter instead, using the value encoding defined in RFC 5987.
sections.plainLanguage: Names and passwords may contain characters outside ASCII, but both sides have to agree on how they are encoded. The only choice is UTF-8, and the text must be in its normal composed form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HTTP Digest Authentication, when used with human-memorable passwords, is vulnerable to dictionary attacks. Such attacks are much easier than cryptographic attacks on any widely used algorithm, so algorithm agility does not make this usage any more secure. Digest Authentication should therefore be used only with passwords that have a reasonable amount of entropy, for example 128 bits or more, and should be used over a secure channel such as HTTPS.

The scheme requires the authenticating agent to store data derived from the user's name and password in a password file associated with a given realm, normally pairs of username and H(A1). If that file is compromised an attacker gains immediate access to the documents in that realm, and unlike a standard UNIX password file it need not be decrypted to do so. On the other hand, a brute-force attack would be needed to obtain the user's password. This is why the realm is part of the digested data, so that one compromised file does not automatically compromise others, and why the realm string should be unique among the realms a user is likely to use and should include the name of the host doing the authentication. The inability of the client to authenticate the server is a weakness of Digest Authentication.

Digest Authentication does not provide a strong authentication mechanism compared with public-key-based mechanisms, and it offers no confidentiality protection beyond protecting the actual username and password. It offers only limited integrity protection for the messages in either direction: with qop=auth-int the parts of the message used in the calculation are protected, but most header fields and their values could be modified in a man-in-the-middle attack. Many needs for secure HTTP transactions cannot be met by Digest Authentication, and TLS is a more appropriate protocol for those.

An implementation must give special attention to replay attacks with POST and PUT requests. Unless the server employs one-time or otherwise limited-use nonces and insists on qop=auth-int, an attacker could replay valid credentials from a successful request with counterfeit data. An attacker who can eavesdrop can also test overheard nonce and response pairs against a list of common words, and can precompute responses for many common words. The countermeasure against chosen plaintext, precomputed dictionary and batch brute-force attacks is for clients to use the cnonce parameter. The security of the protocol is critically dependent on the randomness of the randomly chosen parameters, such as the client and server nonces, which should be generated by a strong random or properly seeded pseudorandom source.

By modern cryptographic standards, Digest Authentication is weak. But for a large range of purposes it is valuable as a replacement for Basic Authentication, and any compliant implementation will be far superior to Basic Authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is blunt: this scheme is weak by modern standards and should be used over HTTPS with a strong password. It is still much better than Basic, which hands the password over in readable form.

messages.note: No Authorization header field is sent.

messages.label: 401 UNAUTHORIZED WITH WWW-AUTHENTICATE
messages.note: Carries the realm, the nonce, the algorithm and the qop values.

messages.label: GET WITH AUTHORIZATION: DIGEST
messages.note: Carries username, realm, uri, algorithm, nonce, nc, cnonce, qop, response and opaque.

viz.caption: THE RESPONSE FORMULA AND ITS THREE INPUTS AS PRINTED IN RFC 7616

data.title: Computing the response
data.code:
response = <"> < KD ( H(A1), unq(nonce)
                         ":" nc
                         ":" unq(cnonce)
                         ":" unq(qop)
                         ":" H(A2)
                   ) <">

A1       = unq(username) ":" unq(realm) ":" passwd

A2       = Method ":" request-uri

KD(secret, data) = H(concat(secret, ":", data))
